blocks.en: "Coming to Him as to a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God and precious, you also, as living stones, are being built up a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ." — 1 Peter 2:4-5 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Acercándoos a él, piedra viva, desechada ciertamente por los hombres, mas escogida y preciosa para con Dios, vosotros también, como piedras vivas, sois edificados como casa espiritual y sacerdocio santo, para ofrecer sacrificios espirituales, aceptables a Dios por Jesucristo." — 1 Pedro 2:4-5 (RVG)

blocks.en: Newborn Babes, Desiring the Word
blocks.es_reference: Recién Nacidos, Deseando la Palabra

blocks.en: The last unit ended with the new birth through the living word; this one begins with what that newborn life should crave. First, Peter says, there are things to put off: "laying aside all malice, all deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and all evil speaking" (1 Peter 2:1). These are the sins that poison fellowship — the spite, the two-faced word, the jealous heart, the cutting tongue. They have no place in a people born of the truth. And in their place, one great desire: "as newborn babes, desire the pure milk of the word, that you may grow thereby, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious" (1 Peter 2:2-3). A healthy baby cries for milk; it is the surest sign of life. So a healthy believer hungers for the word of God, and by it he grows. The same word that gave the new birth now feeds it. If a person has truly tasted that the Lord is gracious, he will come back to the table again and again.
blocks.es_reference: La última unidad terminó con el nuevo nacimiento por la palabra viva; esta comienza con lo que esa vida recién nacida debe anhelar. Primero, dice Pedro, hay cosas que dejar: "desechando, pues, toda malicia, todo engaño, hipocresía, envidias, y todas las maledicencias" (1 Pedro 2:1). Estos son los pecados que envenenan la comunión — el rencor, la palabra de dos caras, el corazón celoso, la lengua cortante. No tienen lugar en un pueblo nacido de la verdad. Y en su lugar, un gran deseo: "desead, como niños recién nacidos, la leche espiritual no adulterada, para que por ella crezcáis, si es que habéis gustado que el Señor es benigno" (1 Pedro 2:2-3). Un bebé sano llora por leche; es la señal más segura de vida. Así un creyente sano tiene hambre de la palabra de Dios, y por ella crece. La misma palabra que dio el nuevo nacimiento ahora lo alimenta. Si alguien de veras ha gustado que el Señor es benigno, volverá a la mesa una y otra vez.

blocks.en: It is worth weighing the sins Peter names to be put off, for they are not the scandals the world fears most but the quiet poisons of community life: malice, the settled ill-will that wishes another harm; deceit, the crooked word that hides its true intent; hypocrisy, the mask of piety worn over a different heart; envy, the resentment of another’s good; and evil speaking, the tongue that tears down behind a brother’s back. A church may avoid open scandal and still be eaten through by these. Against them Peter sets a single healthy appetite. The pure milk of the word is unmixed and undiluted, free of the additives of human cleverness; and the believer is to crave it as a nursing child craves its mother, not now and then but constantly, for this is how the new life grows.
blocks.es_reference: Vale la pena sopesar los pecados que Pedro nombra para desechar, pues no son los escándalos que el mundo más teme sino los venenos callados de la vida en comunidad: la malicia, la mala voluntad asentada que desea el daño del otro; el engaño, la palabra torcida que esconde su verdadera intención; la hipocresía, la máscara de piedad puesta sobre un corazón distinto; la envidia, el resentimiento del bien ajeno; y la maledicencia, la lengua que derriba a espaldas del hermano. Una iglesia puede evitar el escándalo abierto y aún estar carcomida por estos. Contra ellos Pedro pone un solo apetito sano. La leche pura de la palabra es sin mezcla y sin diluir, libre de los añadidos de la astucia humana; y el creyente ha de anhelarla como el niño de pecho anhela a su madre, no de vez en cuando sino constantemente, pues así crece la vida nueva.

blocks.en: Coming to the Living Stone
blocks.es_reference: Acercándonos a la Piedra Viva

blocks.en: Now Peter changes the picture from a nursery to a building site, and the great theme of the passage appears: stones. He begins with one Stone above all. "Coming to Him as to a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God and precious" (1 Peter 2:4). Christ is the living Stone — living, because He died and rose and can never die again. But notice the strange contradiction the world made of Him: rejected by men, yet chosen by God. Here is the rejected Stone. He came not as a conquering hero, which is what the people wanted, but as a suffering servant, which is what they would not have. One of the saddest verses in the Bible records it: "He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him. But as many as received Him, to them He gave the right to become children of God" (John 1:11-12). His own nation had waited centuries for the Messiah, and when He came they would not have Him; they even charged that His power came from Beelzebub, the devil. Men still reject this Stone. Yet what men threw away, God made precious and chose to be the foundation of everything.
blocks.es_reference: Ahora Pedro cambia el cuadro de una sala de cuna a una obra de construcción, y aparece el gran tema del pasaje: las piedras. Comienza con una Piedra sobre todas. "Acercándoos a él, piedra viva, desechada ciertamente por los hombres, mas escogida y preciosa para con Dios" (1 Pedro 2:4). Cristo es la Piedra viva — viva, porque murió y resucitó y nunca más puede morir. Pero note la extraña contradicción que el mundo hizo de Él: desechado por los hombres, mas escogido por Dios. He aquí la Piedra rechazada. No vino como héroe conquistador, que era lo que el pueblo quería, sino como siervo sufriente, que era lo que no aceptarían. Uno de los versículos más tristes de la Biblia lo registra: "A lo suyo vino, y los suyos no le recibieron. Mas a todos los que le recibieron, les dio potestad de ser hechos hijos de Dios" (Juan 1:11-12). Su propia nación había esperado siglos al Mesías, y cuando vino no lo aceptaron; hasta acusaron que su poder venía de Beelzebú, el diablo. Los hombres aún rechazan esta Piedra. Pero lo que los hombres desecharon, Dios lo hizo precioso y lo escogió para ser el fundamento de todo.

blocks.en: Hold these two words together, for the whole gospel hangs between them: rejected by men, chosen by God. The verdict of men and the verdict of God on the same Stone could not be more opposite. The builders — the religious experts of the day, the men whose business it was to judge stones — looked at Christ and threw Him away as useless. Heaven looked at the same Stone and set it at the very head of the corner. This should steady every believer who finds himself rejected for Christ’s sake. The world’s estimate is not the final word; what men discard, God may treasure. The Stone the builders refused was raised to the place of highest honor, and those who are joined to Him will share in His vindication.
blocks.es_reference: Junte estas dos palabras, pues entre ellas pende todo el evangelio: desechada por los hombres, escogida por Dios. El veredicto de los hombres y el veredicto de Dios sobre la misma Piedra no podrían ser más opuestos. Los edificadores — los expertos religiosos de aquel día, los hombres cuyo oficio era juzgar las piedras — miraron a Cristo y lo desecharon como inútil. El cielo miró la misma Piedra y la puso por cabeza misma del ángulo. Esto debe afirmar a todo creyente que se halla rechazado por causa de Cristo. La estimación del mundo no es la palabra final; lo que los hombres desechan, Dios puede atesorarlo. La Piedra que los edificadores rehusaron fue levantada al lugar de mayor honra, y los que están unidos a Él participarán de su vindicación.

blocks.en: Living Stones, a Spiritual House
blocks.es_reference: Piedras Vivas, una Casa Espiritual

blocks.en: And here is the wonder: those who come to the living Stone become living stones themselves. "You also, as living stones, are being built up a spiritual house, a holy priesthood" (1 Peter 2:5). The lesson draws out three qualities of these living stones. They are divinely chosen — like their Lord, who was chosen by God, the believers are God's elect, not self-made. They are divinely composed — not left lying scattered, but fitted and built together into one house. No single stone is a building; each is set in its place beside the others.
blocks.es_reference: Y he aquí la maravilla: los que se acercan a la Piedra viva llegan a ser piedras vivas ellos mismos. "Vosotros también, como piedras vivas, sois edificados como casa espiritual y sacerdocio santo" (1 Pedro 2:5). La lección señala tres cualidades de estas piedras vivas. Son divinamente escogidas — como su Señor, que fue escogido por Dios, los creyentes son los elegidos de Dios, no hechos por sí mismos. Son divinamente compuestas — no dejadas esparcidas, sino ajustadas y edificadas juntas en una sola casa. Ninguna piedra sola es un edificio; cada una es puesta en su lugar junto a las otras.

blocks.en: The walls of Sparta. A Spartan king once boasted to a visiting monarch about the mighty walls of his city. The visitor looked about and could see no walls at all. "Where are these walls you boast of?" he asked. The king pointed to his bodyguard of magnificent troops and said, "These are the walls of Sparta, and every man of them is a brick." So it is with the church. Its strength is not in stone and mortar but in living people, joined together, each one a brick in the wall, each fitted to the rest.
blocks.es_reference: Las murallas de Esparta. Un rey espartano se jactaba una vez ante un monarca visitante de las poderosas murallas de su ciudad. El visitante miró alrededor y no pudo ver muralla alguna. "¿Dónde están esas murallas de que te jactas?", preguntó. El rey señaló a su guardia de magníficas tropas y dijo: "Estas son las murallas de Esparta, y cada hombre de ellos es un ladrillo." Así es con la iglesia. Su fuerza no está en piedra y argamasa sino en personas vivas, unidas, cada una un ladrillo en la muralla, cada una ajustada a las demás.

blocks.en: And as a holy priesthood, these living stones have work to do: "to offer up spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ" (1 Peter 2:5). This is the priesthood of the believer. Under the old covenant only a few men were priests; now every believer is a priest, with access to God and a sacrifice to bring — the offering of praise, of self, of service — all made acceptable not by our worthiness but through Jesus Christ.
blocks.es_reference: Y como sacerdocio santo, estas piedras vivas tienen una obra que hacer: "ofrecer sacrificios espirituales, aceptables a Dios por Jesucristo" (1 Pedro 2:5). Este es el sacerdocio del creyente. Bajo el antiguo pacto solo unos pocos hombres eran sacerdotes; ahora todo creyente es sacerdote, con acceso a Dios y un sacrificio que traer — la ofrenda de alabanza, de sí mismo, de servicio — todo hecho aceptable no por nuestra dignidad sino por Jesucristo.

blocks.en: The thought of a "holy priesthood" would have astonished these readers. In the temple at Jerusalem only one family could serve as priests, only one tribe could assist them, and only one man could enter the holiest place, and that but once a year. Now Peter tells a scattered company of ordinary believers — slaves and tradesmen and women and the poor among them — that they themselves are priests, every one. They need no human priest to carry their worship to God, for through the one great High Priest each may draw near. And their sacrifices are no longer slain animals but the living offerings of praise, of thanksgiving, of obedient lives laid on the altar, all made acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
blocks.es_reference: La idea de un "sacerdocio santo" habría asombrado a estos lectores. En el templo de Jerusalén solo una familia podía servir como sacerdotes, solo una tribu podía asistirlos, y solo un hombre podía entrar al lugar santísimo, y eso una vez al año. Ahora Pedro dice a una compañía esparcida de creyentes comunes — esclavos y artesanos y mujeres y los pobres entre ellos — que ellos mismos son sacerdotes, cada uno. No necesitan sacerdote humano que lleve su adoración a Dios, pues por medio del único gran Sumo Sacerdote cada uno puede acercarse. Y sus sacrificios ya no son animales degollados sino las ofrendas vivas de alabanza, de acción de gracias, de vidas obedientes puestas sobre el altar, todas hechas aceptables a Dios por Jesucristo.

blocks.en: The Stone the Builders Rejected
blocks.es_reference: La Piedra que Desecharon los Edificadores

blocks.en: To press the point, Peter reaches back into the Old Testament for three sayings about a stone, completing his architecture: the living stones are divinely capped by a chief cornerstone. First, "Behold, I lay in Zion a chief cornerstone, elect, precious, and he who believes on Him will by no means be put to shame" (1 Peter 2:6, citing Isaiah 28:16). The cornerstone sets the line for the whole building; Christ is that stone, and whoever rests on Him will never be ashamed. Second, "The stone which the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone" (1 Peter 2:7, citing Psalm 118:22). The very Stone the experts threw away, God set at the head of the corner. Third, He is "a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense" (1 Peter 2:8, citing Isaiah 8:14). So this one Stone divides all people in two. To those who believe, He is precious, the sure foundation. To those who reject Him, the same Stone becomes the thing they trip over and fall. No one is neutral about this Stone; He is either your cornerstone or your stumbling block.
blocks.es_reference: Para reforzar el punto, Pedro se remonta al Antiguo Testamento por tres dichos acerca de una piedra, completando su arquitectura: las piedras vivas son divinamente coronadas por una principal piedra del ángulo. Primero: "He aquí, pongo en Sion la principal piedra del ángulo, escogida, preciosa; y el que creyere en él, no será avergonzado" (1 Pedro 2:6, citando Isaías 28:16). La piedra angular marca la línea de todo el edificio; Cristo es esa piedra, y quien se apoye en Él nunca será avergonzado. Segundo: "La piedra que desecharon los edificadores, ha venido a ser la cabeza del ángulo" (1 Pedro 2:7, citando Salmo 118:22). La misma Piedra que los expertos desecharon, Dios la puso por cabeza del ángulo. Tercero, Él es "piedra de tropiezo, y roca de escándalo" (1 Pedro 2:8, citando Isaías 8:14). Así que esta sola Piedra divide a todos en dos. Para los que creen, es preciosa, el fundamento seguro. Para los que la rechazan, la misma Piedra viene a ser aquello con que tropiezan y caen. Nadie es neutral ante esta Piedra; es o tu piedra angular o tu piedra de tropiezo.

blocks.en: Notice that the same Stone produces two opposite results, and the difference lies entirely in how a person receives Him. Faith makes the Stone a foundation; unbelief makes the same Stone a snare. Peter does not soften this. Christ cannot be a matter of indifference; to meet Him is to be either built upon Him or broken against Him. The one who believes finds in Him a sure footing that will never give way, so that he is not put to shame. The one who refuses Him stumbles over the very rock of salvation and falls. This is sobering, but it is also clarifying: there is no third option, no neutral ground where a person may admire Christ from a safe distance and remain unchanged.
blocks.es_reference: Note que la misma Piedra produce dos resultados opuestos, y la diferencia está enteramente en cómo la recibe una persona. La fe hace de la Piedra un fundamento; la incredulidad hace de la misma Piedra un lazo. Pedro no lo suaviza. Cristo no puede ser asunto de indiferencia; encontrarse con Él es ser edificado sobre Él o quebrantado contra Él. El que cree halla en Él un apoyo seguro que jamás cederá, de modo que no es avergonzado. El que lo rehusa tropieza en la roca misma de la salvación y cae. Esto es solemne, pero también esclarecedor: no hay tercera opción, ningún terreno neutral donde una persona pueda admirar a Cristo desde una distancia segura y quedar sin cambio.

blocks.en: Chosen People, Royal Priesthood, Holy Nation
blocks.es_reference: Linaje Escogido, Real Sacerdocio, Nación Santa

blocks.en: Peter now gathers up who the believers are in four magnificent titles — the descriptions of God's elect. "But you are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, His own special people" (1 Peter 2:9). Each was once a name for Israel; now Peter lays them on this scattered, suffering church. They are a chosen people — selected by God's own grace. They are a royal priesthood — priests who belong to the King, with access to God Himself. They are a holy nation — a people set apart, citizens of heaven though strangers on earth. And they are His own special people — in older words, a peculiar people, meaning a people God claims as His personal treasure. What a thing to say to believers the world counts as nobodies. And there is a purpose in it: God called them "out of darkness into His marvelous light" so "that you may proclaim the praises of Him who called you" (1 Peter 2:9). They are saved to shine and to speak, declaring the excellencies of the God who rescued them.
blocks.es_reference: Pedro reúne ahora quiénes son los creyentes en cuatro títulos magníficos — las descripciones de los elegidos de Dios. "Mas vosotros sois linaje escogido, real sacerdocio, nación santa, pueblo adquirido" (1 Pedro 2:9). Cada uno fue antes un nombre para Israel; ahora Pedro los pone sobre esta iglesia esparcida y sufriente. Son un pueblo escogido — seleccionados por la propia gracia de Dios. Son un real sacerdocio — sacerdotes que pertenecen al Rey, con acceso a Dios mismo. Son una nación santa — un pueblo apartado, ciudadanos del cielo aunque extranjeros en la tierra. Y son pueblo adquirido — en palabras antiguas, un pueblo peculiar, es decir, un pueblo que Dios reclama como su tesoro personal. ¡Qué cosa decir a creyentes que el mundo tiene por nadie! Y hay un propósito en ello: Dios los llamó "de las tinieblas a su luz admirable" para "que anunciéis las virtudes de aquel que os llamó" (1 Pedro 2:9). Son salvos para brillar y para hablar, declarando las excelencias del Dios que los rescató.

blocks.en: Finally Peter marks the great change that has come over them: "who once were not a people but are now the people of God, who had not obtained mercy but now have obtained mercy" (1 Peter 2:10). Once they were a scattered crowd of strangers, no people at all; now, by mercy, they are the people of God. The exiles of Unit 1 have a family. The whole standing of this church rests not on what they were but on the mercy they have received.
blocks.es_reference: Por último, Pedro marca el gran cambio que ha venido sobre ellos: "vosotros que en tiempo pasado no erais pueblo, pero que ahora sois pueblo de Dios; que en tiempo pasado no habíais alcanzado misericordia, pero ahora habéis alcanzado misericordia" (1 Pedro 2:10). Antes eran una multitud esparcida de extranjeros, ningún pueblo; ahora, por misericordia, son el pueblo de Dios. Los desterrados de la Unidad 1 tienen una familia. Toda la posición de esta iglesia descansa no en lo que eran sino en la misericordia que han recibido.

sa.prompt: Explain verses 1-3 — what believers are to lay aside, and why they should desire the pure milk of the word.
sa.model: Peter first names sins to put off: all malice, deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and evil speaking. These are the very things that poison fellowship among believers, the spite and jealousy and the two-faced word, and they have no place in a people born of the truth. In their place he sets one great desire: like newborn babes, believers are to crave the pure milk of the word. A healthy infant cries for milk, which is the surest sign of life, and so a healthy believer hungers for the word of God. The reason is plain, that they may grow by it. The very word that gave the new birth in the last unit now feeds and grows that new life. And Peter adds a condition, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is gracious; the one who has truly tasted God's goodness will keep coming back to the word again and again.

sa.prompt: Explain what it means that Christ is the living Stone, 'rejected by men but chosen by God' (v.4), drawing on the Rejected Stone theme.
sa.model: Christ is the living Stone, living because He died and rose and can never die again, and Peter sets a sharp contradiction beside Him: He was rejected by men but chosen by God and precious. This is the rejected Stone. He came not as the conquering hero the people wanted but as a suffering servant they would not have. One of the saddest verses in the Bible records it, that He came to His own and His own did not receive Him, yet to all who did receive Him He gave the right to become children of God. His own nation had waited centuries for the Messiah, and when He came they rejected Him, even charging that His power came from Beelzebub the devil. Men still reject this Stone. But what men threw away, God made precious and chose to be the very foundation of His house, so that the world's rejection could not overturn God's choice.

sa.prompt: Explain verse 5 — believers as living stones built into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood — using 'divinely chosen, composed, capped' and the Sparta illustration.
sa.model: Those who come to the living Stone become living stones themselves, being built up into a spiritual house and a holy priesthood. The lesson draws out three qualities. They are divinely chosen, like their Lord who was chosen by God, the elect and not self-made. They are divinely composed, not left scattered but fitted and built together into one house, for no single stone is a building. The Sparta illustration captures this: a king pointed not to walls of mortar but to his soldiers and said these are the walls of the city, and every man of them is a brick; so the church's strength is in living people joined together, each a brick in the wall. And they are divinely capped by the chief cornerstone, Christ Himself, who sets the line for the whole structure. As a holy priesthood they offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ, the priesthood of every believer.

sa.prompt: Explain the stone imagery in verses 6-8 — the chief cornerstone, the rejected stone, and the stone of stumbling.
sa.model: Peter reaches back into the Old Testament for three sayings about a stone. First, God lays in Zion a chief cornerstone, elect and precious, and whoever believes on Him will never be put to shame; the cornerstone sets the line for the whole building, and Christ is that stone. Second, the stone the builders rejected has become the chief cornerstone; the very stone the experts threw away God set at the head of the corner. Third, He is a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense. So this one Stone divides all people into two. To those who believe He is precious, the sure foundation on which they will never be ashamed. But to those who reject Him the same Stone becomes the thing they trip over and fall. No one is neutral before this Stone: He is either your cornerstone, holding your whole life together, or your stumbling block, the rock on which you fall.

sa.prompt: Explain the four titles Peter gives the church in verse 9 (the Descriptions of God's Elect).
sa.model: Peter gathers up the identity of the believers in four magnificent titles, each once a name for Israel and now laid on this scattered, suffering church. They are a chosen people, selected by God's own grace and not by their own worth. They are a royal priesthood, priests who belong to the King and have access to God Himself. They are a holy nation, a people set apart, citizens of heaven though strangers on earth. And they are His own special people, in older words a peculiar people, meaning a people God claims as His personal treasure. These are astonishing names to give to believers the world counts as nobodies. And the titles carry a purpose: God called them out of darkness into His marvelous light so that they may proclaim His praises. They are chosen, royal, holy, and treasured not for their own sake but to shine and to speak the excellencies of the God who saved them.

sa.prompt: According to verse 9, why did God call the church out of darkness into His marvelous light?
sa.model: Peter says God called the church out of darkness into His marvelous light, and he gives the reason: that they may proclaim the praises, or virtues, of Him who called them. The titles of verse 9 are not given so that the church may admire itself; they are given for a purpose. A people once in darkness has been brought into light, and light is meant to shine and be seen. So the church exists to declare God's excellencies, to bear witness to the One who rescued them. Every believer, as part of this chosen and royal people, is to make known the goodness and glory of God before a watching world. This turns even the church's suffering into a stage for praise, for a people who can bless God out of darkness and trial proclaim His worth more loudly than any words of ease could.

sa.prompt: Explain verse 10 — the change from 'not a people' to 'the people of God,' and from no mercy to mercy.
sa.model: Peter marks the great change that has come over the believers. Once they were not a people, a scattered crowd of strangers with no name and no belonging; but now they are the people of God. Once they had not obtained mercy; but now they have obtained mercy. This ties back to the exile identity of the first unit: these wandering strangers, who seemed to belong nowhere, now belong to God Himself and have a family. And Peter is careful about where this new identity rests. It rests not on anything they were or achieved but entirely on the mercy they have received. They did not earn their way into the people of God; mercy brought them in. So the whole standing of this suffering church is grounded in God's free mercy, which means no enemy and no trial can take it away, because what mercy gave, only mercy keeps.

sa.prompt: How does the imagery of newborn babes desiring milk (vv.2-3) connect to being born again through the word in the previous unit?
sa.model: The two units are joined by the word of God. The previous unit ended by saying that believers were born again, not of corruptible seed but incorruptible, through the living word of God. Here Peter takes up the same image of new life and carries it forward: those born again are now newborn babes who must desire the pure milk of that same word in order to grow. The word that gave them life must also nourish it. Just as a baby instinctively craves milk and grows by it, so the new believer should hunger for Scripture and be built up by it day by day. Peter even adds, if you have tasted that the Lord is gracious, the new child who has tasted God's goodness keeps coming back for more. So the word is both the seed of the new birth and the milk of its growth, and a believer who neglects it starves the very life God gave.

sa.prompt: What does it mean that all believers are a 'royal priesthood' (the priesthood of the believer)?
sa.model: To call the church a royal priesthood means that every believer is a priest, not only a special class of clergy. This is the priesthood of the believer. Under the old covenant only certain men could approach God as priests, but now, through Christ, each believer has direct access to God and a sacrifice to bring. The sacrifices are spiritual, the offering of praise, of one's own self, and of service, all made acceptable to God through Jesus Christ rather than by the worshiper's worthiness. The priesthood is royal because these priests belong to the King and share in His dignity. And it means no human mediator stands between the believer and God; Christ alone is the mediator, and through Him the door stands open. So every Christian, however humble, may come boldly to God, worship Him directly, and offer his whole life as a priestly sacrifice of praise.

sa.prompt: Summarize the central message of Unit 4 (1 Peter 2:1-10).
sa.model: Unit 4 builds the church on Christ the living Stone. Laying aside malice and craving the word like newborn babes, believers come to Christ, the Stone rejected by men but chosen by God and precious. They themselves become living stones, divinely chosen, composed together into one spiritual house like the living wall of Sparta, and capped by Christ the chief cornerstone; as a holy priesthood they offer spiritual sacrifices through Him. This one Stone divides all people: precious to those who believe, but a stone of stumbling to those who reject Him. Then Peter crowns the unit with four titles for the church, once names of Israel: a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and God's own special people, called out of darkness into marvelous light to proclaim His praises. Once not a people, they are now the people of God; once without mercy, they have now obtained mercy.
